title: Eye (eyeball)
junior: Your eyes work like cameras. Light goes in through the clear front (cornea) and a small hole (pupil), a lens focuses it, and the retina at the back turns it into messages for your brain.
definition: The adult human eyeball is nearly spherical; its wall has three layers — outer sclera (with the cornea in front), middle choroid (with ciliary body and iris) and inner retina.
structure: Sclera: dense connective tissue; its transparent anterior part is the cornea.
Choroid: bluish, with many blood vessels; thickens in front into the ciliary body, which continues as the pigmented iris around the pupil.
Transparent crystalline lens held by ligaments attached to the ciliary body.
Retina has three layers of neural cells, from inside to outside: ganglion cells, bipolar cells, photoreceptor cells (rods and cones).
Aqueous chamber (between cornea and lens) with aqueous humour; vitreous chamber (between lens and retina) with vitreous humour.
functions: Focuses light onto the retina and converts it into nerve impulses for vision.
neetPoints: Cones: daylight (photopic) and colour vision; three types respond to red, green and blue light.
Rods: twilight (scotopic) vision; contain rhodopsin (visual purple), a derivative of vitamin A.
Fovea (in the macula lutea) has only cones — the point of greatest visual acuity.
commonMistakes: Light passes through ganglion and bipolar cells before reaching photoreceptors — the photoreceptors are the outermost neural layer.

mcqs.stem: The point of greatest visual acuity in the retina is the:
mcqs.explanation: The fovea is densely packed with cones and has no rods.
Rods contain rhodopsin (visual purple), derived from vitamin A.

mcqs.stem: The correct sequence of retinal neural layers from inside (vitreous side) to outside is:
mcqs.explanation: Ganglion cells are innermost; photoreceptors are outermost, next to the pigment layer.

title: Cornea
junior: The cornea is the clear window at the front of your eye. It bends light to help focus it.
definition: The cornea is the transparent anterior portion of the sclera.
structure: Avascular (no blood vessels); receives oxygen from air and aqueous humour.
Richly supplied with sensory nerves.
functions: Admits light and does most of the eye's refraction.
neetPoints: Because the cornea is avascular, corneal transplants are rarely rejected by the immune system.

mcqs.stem: The cornea is a modification of the:
mcqs.explanation: It is the transparent anterior part of the sclera.

mcqs.stem: Corneal transplants are seldom rejected because the cornea is:
mcqs.explanation: With no blood vessels, immune cells rarely reach the graft.

title: Lens
junior: The lens is a clear, bendy disc behind your pupil. Tiny muscles change its shape so you can focus on things near and far.
definition: The lens is a transparent, biconvex crystalline structure held by ligaments (suspensory ligaments) attached to the ciliary body.
structure: Elastic capsule; no blood vessels.
Separates the aqueous chamber (front) from the vitreous chamber (behind).
functions: Fine focusing (accommodation) by changing its curvature.
neetPoints: Cataract is clouding of the lens.

mcqs.stem: The lens of the eye is held in position by ligaments attached to the:
mcqs.explanation: Suspensory ligaments connect the lens to the ciliary body.

mcqs.stem: The chamber between the lens and the retina contains:
mcqs.explanation: The vitreous chamber is filled with transparent gel called vitreous humour.

title: Retina
junior: The retina is a thin layer at the back of your eye, full of light-sensing cells called rods and cones. Rods help you see in dim light; cones see colours.
definition: The retina is the innermost layer of the eyeball containing photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) and neurons.
structure: Layers of ganglion, bipolar and photoreceptor cells.
Blind spot (optic disc) medial to and slightly above the posterior pole.
Macula lutea with the fovea lateral to the blind spot.
functions: Converts light into nerve impulses: light dissociates retinal from opsin, changing membrane permeability and generating potentials.
neetPoints: Light induces dissociation of retinal from opsin, causing a structural change in opsin and generating action potentials.

mcqs.stem: Photopigments in photoreceptors are composed of opsin and:
mcqs.explanation: Photopigments are made of opsin (protein) and retinal (aldehyde of vitamin A).

mcqs.stem: Twilight (scotopic) vision is the function of:
mcqs.explanation: Rods are responsible for vision in dim light.

title: Iris and pupil
junior: The iris is the coloured part of your eye. It's a ring of muscle that makes the pupil (the black hole in the middle) smaller in bright light and bigger in the dark.
definition: The iris is the pigmented, opaque continuation of the ciliary body; the aperture it surrounds is the pupil.
structure: Sphincter (circular) and dilator (radial) muscle fibres.
Pigment gives eye colour.
functions: Regulates the diameter of the pupil and so the amount of light entering the eye.
neetPoints: The iris is the visible coloured portion of the eye; pupil diameter is regulated by its muscle fibres.

mcqs.stem: The diameter of the pupil is regulated by:
mcqs.explanation: Sphincter and dilator muscles of the iris control pupil size.

mcqs.stem: The iris is a continuation of the:
mcqs.explanation: The ciliary body continues forward as the pigmented iris.

title: Sclera
junior: The sclera is the tough white outer coat of your eyeball. It protects the eye and keeps its round shape.
definition: The sclera is the outer layer of the eyeball composed of dense connective tissue.
structure: Continuous in front with the transparent cornea.
Extra-ocular muscles are attached to it.
functions: Protects the eye and maintains its shape.
neetPoints: Eyeball wall layers from outside: sclera → choroid → retina.

mcqs.stem: The outermost layer of the eyeball is the:
mcqs.explanation: The sclera is the outer dense connective-tissue coat.

mcqs.stem: The middle, bluish, vascular layer of the eyeball is the:
mcqs.explanation: The choroid contains many blood vessels and looks bluish.

title: External ear (pinna)
junior: The outer ear, or pinna, is the curly part you can see. It collects sounds and funnels them into the ear canal towards your eardrum.
definition: The outer ear consists of the pinna and the external auditory meatus (canal); the meatus leads inwards to the tympanic membrane (eardrum).
structure: Pinna: elastic cartilage covered by skin.
Very fine hairs and wax-secreting sebaceous glands in the skin of the pinna and meatus.
Middle ear: ossicles malleus (attached to the tympanic membrane), incus and stapes (attached to the oval window of the cochlea); Eustachian tube connects to the pharynx.
Inner ear: cochlea with the organ of Corti (hair cells on the basilar membrane) and the vestibular apparatus (three semicircular canals and the otolith organ — saccule and utricle).
functions: Pinna collects vibrations in the air that produce sound.
Cochlea: hearing; vestibular apparatus: balance and posture.
neetPoints: The Eustachian tube helps equalise pressure on either side of the eardrum.
Ear ossicles increase the efficiency of transmission of sound waves to the inner ear.
Crista ampullaris (semicircular canals) and macula (saccule, utricle) are the receptors for balance.

mcqs.stem: The ear ossicle attached to the tympanic membrane is the:
mcqs.explanation: The malleus is attached to the tympanic membrane; the stapes to the oval window.

mcqs.stem: The organ of Corti is located on the:
mcqs.explanation: It contains hair cells that act as auditory receptors.

mcqs.stem: Which structure equalises air pressure on both sides of the eardrum?
mcqs.explanation: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear cavity with the pharynx.
